L18@P1: Abstract: This paper attempts to document and account for the long run evolution of
L19@P1: inheritance. We find that in a country like France the annual flow of inheritance was
L20@P1: about 20%-25% of national income between 1820 and 1910, down to less than 5% in
L21@P1: 1950, and back up to about 15% by 2010. A simple theoretical model of wealth
L22@P1: accumulation, growth and inheritance can fully account for the observed U-shaped
L23@P1: pattern and levels. Using this model, we find that under plausible assumptions the
L24@P1: annual bequest flow might reach about 20%-25% of national income by 2050. This
L25@P1: corresponds to a capitalized bequest share in total wealth accumulation well above
L26@P1: 100%. Our findings illustrate the fact that when the growth rate g is small, and when
L27@P1: the rate of return to private wealth r is permanently and substantially larger than the
L28@P1: growth rate (say, r=4%-5% vs. g=1%-2%), which was the case in the 19th century and
L29@P1: early 20th century and is likely to happen again in the 21st century, then past wealth
L30@P1: and inheritance are bound to play a key role for aggregate wealth accumulation and
L31@P1: the structure of lifetime inequality. Contrarily to a widely spread view, modern
L32@P1: economic growth did not kill inheritance.

L65@P3: 1. Introduction
L66@P3: There are basically two ways to become rich: either through one’s own work, or through
L67@P3: inheritance. In Ancien Regime societies, as well as during the 19th century and early 20th
L68@P3: century, it was self-evident to everybody that the inheritance channel was an important
L69@P3: one. For instance, 19th century and early 20th century novels are full of stories where
L70@P3: ambitious young men have to choose between becoming rich through their own work or by
L71@P3: marrying a bride with large inherited wealth – and often opt for the second strategy.
L72@P3: However, in the late 20th century and early 21st century, most observers seem to believe
L73@P3: that this belongs to the past. That is, most observers – novelists, economists and laymen
L74@P3: alike – tend to assume that labor income is now playing a much bigger role than inherited
L75@P3: wealth in shaping people’s lives, and that human capital and hard work have become the
L76@P3: key to personal material well-being. Although this is rarely formulated explicitly, the implicit
L77@P3: assumption seems to be that the structure of modern economic growth has led to the rise
L78@P3: of human capital, the decline of inheritance, and the triumph of meritocracy.
L79@P3: This paper asks a simple question: is this optimistic view of economic development
L80@P3: justified empirically and well-grounded theoretically? Our simple answer is “no”. Our
L81@P3: empirical and theoretical findings suggest that inherited wealth will most likely play as big a
L82@P3: role in 21st century capitalism as it did in 19th century capitalism – at least from an
L83@P3: aggregate viewpoint.
L84@P3: This paper makes two contributions. First, by combining various data sources in a
L85@P3: systematic manner, we document and establish a simple – but striking – fact: the
L86@P3: aggregate inheritance flow has been following a very pronounced U-shaped pattern in
L87@P3: France since the 19th century. To our knowledge, this is the first time that such long-run,
L88@P3: homogenous inheritance series are constructed for any country.
L89@P3: More precisely, we define the annual inheritance flow as the total market value of all
L90@P3: assets (tangible and financial assets, net of financial liabilities) transmitted at death or
L91@P3: through inter-vivos gifts during a given year.1
L92@P3:  We find that the annual inheritance flow was

L127@P4:  Whether one should use national or disposable income as denominator is a matter of perspective. If one
L128@P4: assumes that government expenditures are useless, and that the rise of government during the 20th century
L129@P4: has limited the ability of private individuals to save, accumulate and transmit private wealth, then one should
L130@P4: use disposable income. But to the extent that government expenditures are mostly useful (e.g. assuming that
L131@P4: in the absence of public spending in health and education, then individuals would have to had to pay at least
L132@P4: as much to buy similar services on the market), it seems more justified to use national income. One
L133@P4: additional advantage of using national income is that it tends to be better measured. Disposable income can
L134@P4: display large time-series and cross-country variations for purely definitional reasons. E.g. in France,
L135@P4: disposable income would jump from 70% to about 80% of national income if one includes in-kind health

L140@P5: The second – and most important – contribution of this paper is to account for these facts,
L141@P5: and to draw lessons for other countries and for the future. We show that a simple
L142@P5: theoretical model of wealth accumulation, growth and inheritance can easily explain why
L143@P5: the French inheritance flow seems to return to a high steady-state value around 20% of
L144@P5: national income. Consider first a dynastic model where all savings come from capital
L145@P5: income. Wealth holders save a fraction g/r of their asset returns, so that aggregate private
L146@P5: wealth Wt and national income Yt grow at the same rate g, and the wealth-income ratio
L147@P5: β=Wt/Yt is stationary. It is straightforward to prove that the steady-state inheritance flownational income ratio is equal to by=β/H, where H is generation length (average age at
L148@P5: parenthood). If β=600% and H=30, then by=20%. We show that this intuition can be
L149@P5: generalized to more general saving models. Namely, as long as the (real) growth rate g is
L150@P5: sufficiently small and the (real) rate of return on private wealth r is sufficiently large – say,
L151@P5: g=1%-2% vs. r=4%-5% –, then steady-state by is close to the class saving level β/H.
L152@P5: The key intuition boils down to a simple r>g logic. In countries with large growth, such as
L153@P5: France during the 1950s-1970s, then wealth coming from the past (i.e. accumulated or
L154@P5: received by one’s parents or grand-parents, who were relatively poor as compared to
L155@P5: today’s incomes) does not matter too much. What counts is new wealth accumulated out
L156@P5: of current income. Inheritance flows are bound to be a small fraction of national income.
L157@P5: But in countries with low growth, such as France in the 19th century and since the 1970s,
L158@P5: the logic is reversed. With low growth, successors simply need to save a small fraction of
L159@P5: their asset returns in order to ensure that their inherited wealth grows at least as fast as
L160@P5: national income. In effect, g small and r>g imply that wealth coming from the past is being
L161@P5: capitalized at a faster rate than national income. So past wealth tends to dominate new
L162@P5: wealth, rentiers tend to dominate labor income earners, and inheritance flows are large
L163@P5: relative to national income. As g→0, then by → β/H – irrespective of saving behavior.
